subject: small N-mix dataset and GOF test

messages.author: 772b61569d258fdf
messages.subject: small N-mix dataset and GOF test
parts:
Hi everyone!

I have a question regarding the application of N-mixture models (single season pcount) to small datasets and the behaviour of the goodness of fit test (Nmix.gof.test in package AICcmodavg) in this situation.

I’ve read a recent publication in which pcount is used to obtain density estimates of Italian cave salamanders from 7 sites (caves) surveyed 5 times. Authors obtain very precise estimates (narrow CI) of density for each site using empirical Bayes method (ranef), but they did not report a goodness of fit test.

With similar datasets i hardly obtain good model fit, nor reliable estimates.

I downloaded the dataset provided along with the paper and tried to run a gof test with the following results:


 Chi-square goodness-of-fit for N-mixture model of 'unmarkedFitPCount' class

 

Observed chi-square statistic = 1513.685 

Number of bootstrap samples = 5000

P-value = 0

 

Quantiles of bootstrapped statistics:

   0%   25%   50%   75%  100% 

  8.7  23.9  30.0  38.0 104.4 

 

Estimate of c-hat = 47.46 

 

The results clearly indicate lack of fit: how much a similar over-dispersion affect the density estimates? Is it possible that the small dataset exacerbated the results obtained from gof test?

In similar situations (small dataset) are there any other ways to assess fit of N-mixture models?

I enclose the dataset if someone is interested.

 

Thank you in advance for any suggestion!


Andrea

messages.author: 4e956cc50ac3e075
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] small N-mix dataset and GOF test
parts:
Hi Andrea,

this is not necessarily specific to the chi-square goodness of fit test
implemented in AICcmodavg. With a total of only 7 sites and the "rogue"
site 5 with extreme values compared to the other 6 sites, it is not
surprising to experience lack-of-fit. The test is simply saying that it
is difficult to simulate a data set with the same characteristics as
those observed in your data based on the parameters estimated in the
original model. Regarding the c-hat you report, moderate deviations
from 1 (< ~ 3 - 4) suggest that lack-of-fit is due to overdispersion,
but that the model may still be adequate. A c-hat ~ 40 (similar to the
one you report) rather suggests that the lack-of-fit observed is not
only a result of overdispersion, but that the model structure is
inappropriate.

You could set up a small simulation to see how the number of sites
influences your ability to estimate the parameters in the model and
their variance by progressively increasing the number of sites. There
are already a number of very useful resources out there to help you
through it, starting with Andy's 2004 paper (Royle, J. A. 2004. N-
mixture models for estimating population size from spatially replicated
counts. Biometrics 60:108-115), and a number of good books such as:
Kéry, M. 2010. Introduction to WinBUGS for ecologists: a Bayesian
approach to regression, ANOVA, mixed models and related analyses.
Academic Press, New York, USA.
Kéry, M., and J. A. Royle. 2016. Applied hierarchical modeling in
ecology: analysis of distribution, abundance and species richness in R
and BUGS. Academic Press, New York, USA.

Hope it helps,

Marc

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: small N-mix dataset and GOF test
parts:
Hi Vy,

If you haven't already, I suggest starting by reading up on N-mixture
models and overdispersion in Marc Kéry and Andy Royle's book: Applied
hierarchical modelling in ecology vol 1.

The nmixgof package has some nice functions and graphical diagnostics
to investigate different sources of overdispersion.

Best,

Marc
